transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-26
Start: 10:00 AM UTC
Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood CSM); Mark Reynolds (BrightBank Head of ML), Sofia Martinez (BrightBank Infra), Daniel Kim (BrightBank PM)

Summary: quick review of last week's KV/prefix caching results, discuss prompt reuse strategies and canonicalization, decide on next benchmarks and who runs them.

[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining, do we have any quick updates before we dive straight into numbers?
[00:10] Mark: no, chief, go ahead, we were looking forward to the hit-rate numbers you sent last night.
[00:16] Alex: cool. Priya, you wanna take us through the dashboard?
[00:20] Priya: yep, i'll share screen in a sec, so last week's run with the current canonicalization pipeline returned about a 62% KV hit rate overall across the sample workload. with template normalization and prompt reuse heuristics enabled, peak went to ~78% on the 1k context experiments. i'll paste the per-prefix breakdown in chat after.
[00:40] Daniel: sorry, when you say 62% overall, that's across all prefixes? or is that per-session?
[00:45] Priya: its overall across the 10k queries we ran, aggregated by prefix family. some prefixes are much higher - like auth flows were 92% - but long-form support prompts are closer to 20%.
[01:02] Sofia: and the tail latency impact? we saw some spikes in previous runs.
[01:06] Priya: good call - p95 token gen latency was about 420ms for cache hits vs 1.8s for misses on our bench infra. p99 for misses went up to nearly 3.1s. so hit-rate matters a lot for the user experience. keep in mind infra is a bit smaller than your prod config so numbers are directional.
[01:28] Mark: right that's helpful. can you remind us what the caching key looks like? we had a conversation about including user id vs session id.
[01:34] Alex: yeah current key is hash(normalize(template) + conversation_prefix + model+version) - we avoid user-specific identifiers to keep hit-rate across users higher, but for strict privacy we can use salted hashes.
[01:50] Daniel: normalize(template) - what's in normalization? removing timestamps, numeric IDs, whitespace, lowercasing?
[01:56] Priya: exactly those things, plus removing stop-words in the instruction and collapsing multi-space. we also apply a light paraphrase canonicalizer that matches common variants (like please -> pls in the training set). it's imperfect; we saw some mismatches where paraphrase broke a slot.
[02:15] Mark: are you running any semantic matching for near-misses? like getting the same answer when prompt wording changes slightly?
[02:20] Priya: not in the primary cache path - it's exact key matching on the canonicalized prompt. we experimented with an approximate match using embedding distance but that added 20% additional CPU and complexity. might be a good hybrid for low-latency cold path.
[02:36] Jordan: quick question from the ops side - how are you handling KV cache TTLs and eviction?
[02:40] Priya: default TTL is 24h, eviction is LRU within each shard. we tested shorter TTLs (6h) and that dropped hit-rate by 7% but reduced staleness for time-sensitive tasks.
[02:52] Sofia: for BrightBank, we care about staleness for pricing prompts - 24h might be too long, could we do per-prefix TTLs?
[02:58] Priya: yes, that's one of the config knobs we suggested - per-prefix TTLs. short TTL for pricing, longer for canned responses.
[03:08] Alex: let's walk through a couple of specific prefix families and see where the biggest gains are. Priya, can you go to the "auth" and "support" sheets?
[03:14] Priya: sharing... auth is 92% hit-rate as i said; support long-form is 18%. the middle category (policy/faq style) is around 65%. if we focus on support long-form, the main issue is prompt variability - users rewrite the same question many ways.
[03:33] Mark: do you have recommendations for reducing variability? we can't restrict user text.
[03:36] Priya: two strategies: 1) enforce template-based prompts from the client side (server-side instrumentation to rewrite variants to canonical template); 2) fuzzy prefix matching using an embedding index to route similar prompts to same cached response if confidence is high. client-side normalization gave the biggest lift in our bench.
[03:55] Daniel: embedding-based routing worries me for cost and false positives though.
[03:59] Priya: yup, cost tradeoff - you pay for the extra embed query and compute, but you can limit it to only low-frequency prefixes.
[04:10] Sofia: what's the bandwidth impact for caching large completions? some of our support responses are 3-4k tokens. are you storing whole completions in Redis?
[04:16] Priya: we store compressed blobs and also option to store deltas for long outputs. storage at bench was about 1.6GB for 10k responses with 200 avg tokens. for 3-4k token responses we recommend object store + index pointer in cache.
[04:33] Mark: interesting. what about consistency when we roll models - do cached responses stay valid?
[04:38] Alex: good question. our rollout strategy is to namespace by model+version in the cache key so when you change model the hits automatically invalidate. we also support warm-starting new model with shadow traffic and pre-populating cache with golden prompts.
[04:54] Priya: also to add - we can create a regression detector that watches a subset of cached responses when model changes, to flag quality regressions.
[05:03] Mark: can we see the regression detector config in the docs?
[05:06] Alex: yes, i'll send that doc.
[05:10] Priya: back to numbers - we ran an A/B where we enabled client normalization on 30% of traffic and saw end-to-end token cost reduction of 21% and weighted latency improvement of ~35%.
[05:22] Daniel: wow that's compelling. for POC success metrics, we said >50% hit-rate on primary 3 prefixes and p95 < 500ms - are we on track?
[05:31] Priya: for auth and faq yes, support long-form is lagging. overall we meet the >50% target. p95 is around 420ms on hits in bench.
[05:40] Mark: ok so practical asks: 1) can you run a 16k context KV run to reflect our long chat sessions? 2) can you provide per-prefix TTL suggestions and a config we can test?
[05:51] Priya: yes to both. the 16k run needs slightly different bench config - i'll add it to action items.
[05:58] Alex: also remember we saw some transcription weirdness in prior recordings where "KV cash" was transcribed; we'll keep those notes but it's fine.
[06:04] (laughter)
[06:06] Sofia: a question on security - are any user identifiers present in the cache keys in your POC? if so we need to see KMS and salt plans.
[06:15] Alex: we do not store raw user ids. we can use per-customer salt and HMAC to satisfy privacy and still get multi-user hits if needed. our Private deployment supports customer-controlled KMS for key material.
[06:28] Sofia: can you send us a short note on how salted hashing works for cache keys and compliance implications?
[06:33] Alex: yes will include in the doc pack.
[06:36] Priya: quick technical note - for 16k context we need to ensure KV cache sharding works with bigger KV items; eviction heuristics might need to be tuned to avoid OOM. i'll include expected memory profile in the bench results.
[06:50] Daniel: and if the cache grows too big, do you have an auto-prune or bloom-filter approach?
[06:55] Priya: we can use bloom filters to avoid unnecessary lookups for cold prefixes and also have scheduled compaction jobs.
[07:02] Alex: moving on, let's agree who runs what. Priya will do the 16k bench and include per-prefix hit-rates and tail latencies. Sofia will confirm infra limits. Mark will gather the 500-query prompt set. Alex will send canonicalization and the regression detector doc.
[07:18] Mark: sounds good. a small note - when you hash key, can you include a deterministic truncate to make redis keys shorter?
[07:24] Priya: yes we use base64-url of sha256 and then truncate to 24 chars by default; we can shorten if you need.
[07:31] Daniel: any risk of collisions?
[07:33] Priya: negligible at truncation lengths we use, but we can switch to longer if you're paranoid.
[07:39] Jordan: okay folks, timeline recap? next sync same time next week?
[07:43] Alex: yes, next Wednesday same time. Priya will report bench results and we'll look at dashboards.
[07:48] Mark: one more ask - can you also produce a CSV with per-prefix counts so we can slice by user cohort?
[07:54] Priya: yes i'll include CSV export.
[07:57] Alex: great. any final questions?
[08:00] Mark: none here, thanks everyone.
[08:03] Sofia: thanks.
[08:05] Alex: thanks team, we'll follow-up in email with artifacts.

Recap / Next steps:
- Priya: run 16k context KV benchmark and share detailed per-prefix hit-rate + tail latency CSV by 2026-06-02.
- Sofia: confirm infra / VPC limits and available dedicated pool burst by 2026-06-01.
- Alex: share canonicalization and regression detector docs by 2026-05-28.
- Mark: provide 500-query representative prompt set by 2026-05-29.

References mentioned: canonicalization examples (link sent in chat), bench dashboards (internal link), cache_key_hmac.md (to be shared).

End of transcript.
